messages.author: 6f84786b4d90ec96
messages.subject: Re: model choice
parts:
Looks like the way you setup your models in Program Distance resulted in it
selecting the same model 4-times (probably for one key function) and the
same model 2-times (probably for some other key function). You have got to
check out the output to see which model was selected for each analysis or
model run... Looks like you have got fairly poor model fit as well;
probably need to investigate why...

Matt

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: model choice
parts:
Quite right Matt.

Also, Brett, AIC is designed to account for the effect of additional parameters,
so all other things being equal, the lowest AIC model is the best choice. As
Matt said, you need to check the model fit. All of this is detailed in the
Introduction to Distance Sampling book - see particularly section 2.5 for advice
on how to proceed with analysis (this section is also in the Distance manual
(page on CDS Analysis Guidelines) and I think in the Thomas et al. (2010) paper
on Distance).

Note that it is not always advisable to choose the lowest AIC model, if you have
other reasons to think an alternative model produces more plausible estimates --
for an example of this that I'm familiar with, see the analysis for Pacific
white-sided dolphin in Williams and Thomas (2007). Lastly, uncertainty about
detection function model selection can be incorporated into the analysis, via a
bootstrap (also in the Introduction to Distance sampling book somewhere; see
also the manual page on Model Averaging in CDS Analysis, and Williams and Thomas
(2009) for an example).

Cheers, - Len

Williams, R. and L. Thomas. 2007. Distribution and abundance of marine mammals
in the coastal waters of British Columbia, Canada. Journal of Cetacean Research
and Management 9: 15-28.
Available from http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/WilliamsJCRM2007.pdf
